Building Stella: What It Actually Does
A high-level introduction to Stella, a speech practice platform for children ages 3-8.

I keep describing Stella in a different way depending on who is asking, which is usually a sign
that I have not written the plain version down yet. So here it is: what Stella is, what a child
actually does with it, and what happens behind the scenes.

## The short version

Stella is a speech practice platform for children roughly ages 3-8. A child plays a few short
games on an iPad, saying words out loud. Stella listens, scores each individual sound in each
word, and uses that history to choose what the child practises next time.

That last part is the whole idea. The app is not a fixed word list dressed up as a game. The set
of picture cards a child gets is picked for that child, from what we have heard them say so far.

## The problem it's aimed at

Speech sound practice works when it happens often and in small doses. The constraint is rarely
knowledge, it is logistics. A child might see a speech-language pathologist once a week for half
an hour, and the rest of the progress depends on practice at home, where nobody has a phoneme
inventory in their head and everyone is tired by 7pm.

Two things tend to go wrong with home practice. It stops happening, because it is a chore. And
when it does happen, it drills whatever is on the printed sheet rather than what the child is
currently struggling with.

Stella tries to remove both. The child sees a game. The parent does not have to decide anything.
The choice of what to practise is made from evidence rather than a guess.

## What a child actually does

Right now there are three games in a child's hands, and they unlock in a sequence, because you
cannot personalize practice for a child you have never heard speak.

**Balloon Pop** comes first, and it is deliberately not scored. Picture cards float up one at a
time, the child names what they see, and the balloon pops either way. Nothing to pass or fail on
the first day. What we get out of it is a baseline: a first recording of how this child sounds.

**Pizza Luca** is the practice loop. Luca runs a pizzeria, the child says the target word, and a
clear attempt earns a star and a pizza topping. A missed attempt just comes back around later.
This is where most of the scored practice happens.

**Which Word?** is the listening game, and it needs no microphone at all. The child hears one of
two very similar words, "cub" and "tub" say, and taps the picture that matches. Hearing the
difference between two sounds generally comes before reliably producing it, so this fills a real
gap rather than being a break from the "real" games.

A few more are in development, including one where the child reads a target word inside a full
sentence, and one where they sort word cards by which sound they contain.

## What happens underneath

The flow, at the altitude that matters:

1. **Record.** The child says a word. The audio goes to the backend.
2. **Score every sound, not the word.** The word "sun" does not come back as one number. It comes
   back as three: the /s/, the /u/ and the /n/, each on a 0-100 scale. This is the part that makes
   everything downstream possible.
3. **Build a profile.** Those per-sound scores accumulate. Over time you get "this child gets /s/
   right about a third of the time, and /l/ nearly always", with a minimum number of attempts
   before any sound is allowed to count, so a single bad recording never labels a child.
4. **Choose the next words.** Each candidate word is scored by how much it would help _this_
   child, which mostly means: does it practise a sound they are missing, and does it practise it
   in the position where they actually lose it. If a child only drops /s/ at the end of words,
   "bus" is worth more to them than "sun".
5. **Serve a round.** Two targeted cards, one free card drawn from the whole pool.

That free card is the least obvious decision and one of the more important ones. If every card
came from a child's current problem list, we would never find out that a sound has been fixed, or
that a sound nobody has tested yet is a problem. The only way to learn anything new is to ask a
question you do not already know the answer to.

The parent side of the app turns the same data into a report: which sounds are strong, which are
weak, what changed since last week.

## What it is not

Stella supports speech practice. It is not an evaluation, it is not a diagnosis, and it does not
replace a speech-language pathologist. The ranked list of a child's weakest sounds is a _ranking_:
every child has ten weakest sounds, including a child who is doing fine. Reading that list as a
clinical judgement would be a mistake, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than in the
footnotes.

There are also real limits that are not about the software. The single biggest one is artwork.
Every word we can serve needs a picture and a prompt recording, and today the illustrated
vocabulary is a small fraction of the words we have prepared. A child who struggles with a sound
we have no pictures for cannot be given targeted practice for it, no matter how good the
selection logic is.

That gap between "the system knows what to do" and "the system has what it needs to do it" turns
out to be most of what I spend time on. More on that in the next one.

This theme comes with the [@astrojs/mdx](https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/mdx/) integration installed and configured in your `astro.config.mjs` config file. If you prefer not to use MDX, you can disable support by removing the integration from your config file.

## Why MDX?

MDX is a special flavor of Markdown that supports embedded JavaScript & JSX syntax. This unlocks the ability to [mix JavaScript and UI Components into your Markdown content](https://docs.astro.build/en/guides/integrations-guide/mdx/#mdx-in-astro) for things like interactive charts or alerts.

If you have existing content authored in MDX, this integration will hopefully make migrating to Astro a breeze.

## Example

Here is how you import and use a UI component inside of MDX.  
When you open this page in the browser, you should see the clickable button below.

import HeaderLink from "../../components/HeaderLink.astro";

<HeaderLink href="#" onclick="alert('clicked!')">
  Embedded component in MDX
</HeaderLink>

## More Links

- [MDX Syntax Documentation](https://mdxjs.com/docs/what-is-mdx)
- [Astro Usage Documentation](https://docs.astro.build/en/basics/astro-pages/#markdownmdx-pages)
- **Note:** [Client Directives](https://docs.astro.build/en/reference/directives-reference/#client-directives) are still required to create interactive components. Otherwise, all components in your MDX will render as static HTML (no JavaScript) by default.
